name: Cinnamon / apple cider vinegar shots

lead: ACV shots are small servings of diluted apple cider vinegar, sometimes mixed with cinnamon, drunk to reduce bloating, help fat loss and clear skin. Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting pressed apple juice to alcohol and then to acetic acid, and is about 5% acetic acid.

The chain: proponents attribute effects to acetic acid, which they say curbs appetite and moderates blood sugar, leading to a leaner midsection. Wikipedia reports no high-quality clinical evidence that regular use affects body weight, blood sugar or lipids, and that health organizations do not recommend it as a therapy.

paras: People mix a small amount of vinegar into water, sometimes adding cinnamon, and drink it daily, often before meals. Users report judging effects over several weeks.

Diluted moderate use is generally described as low-risk. Reported harms include tooth-enamel erosion, throat and esophageal irritation, digestive upset, and burns when applied to skin or eyes. Possible interactions with insulin and diuretics are noted.

angle.text: Home-made apple cider vinegar shots, sometimes with cinnamon, are taken to reduce bloating, curb appetite and clear skin, with a leaner midsection as the goal. The effect is attributed to acetic acid. Reviews report no high-quality trials of regular use for weight.

lead: Cinnamon and apple cider vinegar (ACV) shots are a home-made drink in which diluted apple cider vinegar, sometimes with cinnamon, is swallowed in the belief that it helps with fat loss, bloating or skin. Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting pressed apple juice first to alcohol and then to acetic acid, and is about 5% acetic acid and 94% water.[1]

Claimed benefits include weight loss, blood-sugar and cholesterol control and skin improvement. The Wikipedia article on apple cider vinegar reports no high-quality clinical evidence that regular use helps with body weight or with blood glucose and lipid levels, and says major public health organizations and regulators do not recommend it as a therapy.[1] Documented risks of undiluted or excessive use include tooth-enamel erosion and throat irritation.[1]
infobox: Fat loss, appetite, blood sugar, skin

paras: Apple cider vinegar is produced when yeast ferments the sugars in apple juice to ethanol and acetic acid bacteria then convert the ethanol to acetic acid. Unfiltered products may contain a cloudy cellulose-rich biofilm called the mother.[1] A typical 'shot' preparation involves a small amount of vinegar diluted in water, sometimes with ground cinnamon, honey or lemon added for taste.
Apple cider vinegar has been used in cooking and food preservation for centuries, and vinegars from North Atlantic fruits became popular in the early nineteenth century.[1]

Proponents promote the drink for weight loss, reduced appetite, lower blood glucose and lipids, and for skin clarity. Wikipedia notes these are the principal claimed health uses and that evidence for them is poor.[1]
Cinnamon is added by some users on the belief that it also supports blood-sugar control; this article does not rely on any source evaluating cinnamon's effects on appearance.

Moderate, diluted consumption is generally regarded as low-risk, according to the summary on Wikipedia.[1] Reported problems include tooth-enamel damage and increased dentin sensitivity from excessive intake, esophageal injury from incompletely swallowed tablets, and digestive effects such as burping and flatulence.[1]

Applying vinegar directly to skin or eyes has been associated with irritation, burns and possible corneal injury.[1] The article also notes possible interactions with insulin and diuretics, that use may be unsafe in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and that some brands have shown inconsistent acid levels.[1]

No studies of the combined cinnamon and apple cider vinegar shot for appearance outcomes were found. A 2020 systematic review by Launholt, Kristiansen and Hjorth in the European Journal of Nutrition examined the safety, side effects and effects of apple cider vinegar on metabolic parameters and body weight; Wikipedia cites it as its main review on the topic.[1]
